title: Eutychus (Acts 20:7–12)
hook: a young man falls asleep during Paul's long sermon and falls from a window

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tentmakers, Priscilla and Aquila, taking Apollos aside. Your line was more perfectly. Did you teach anyone gently? Day five hundred fifty-three.

If you have ever fought to stay awake through a long homily, a lecture, or a work meeting that should have been an email, this story is for you. It's in the Bible. And the long speaker isn't some dull preacher. It's the Apostle Paul. And the listener who nods off is a young man named Eutychus, sitting in an open window, three floors up. What happens next is both funny and serious.
screen: `A LONG HOMILY.` → `THE SPEAKER IS PAUL.` → `A YOUNG MAN IN A WINDOW.`

segments.voice: It's Troas, a port on the coast of what is now Turkey. Luke sets the scene carefully. In the King James: "upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread." Sunday. The church gathered for the breaking of the bread. Paul is leaving the next day, so he has a lot to say, and he keeps talking until midnight. The upper room is crowded, and there are many lamps burning, which means it's warm and close and smoky. A young man named Eutychus is sitting in the window. And the text, with a straight face, says he sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on, and fell from the third story, and was taken up dead. Everyone rushes down. Paul goes down too, throws himself on the young man, embraces him, and says: don't be troubled, his life is in him. And then the part that makes people laugh. Paul goes back upstairs, breaks the bread, eats, and keeps talking until daybreak. Even after a man fell out the window, even Paul went on. Meanwhile they bring the young man home alive, and the text says they were not a little comforted. His name, Eutychus, means fortunate. Luke may be smiling. But under the humor is one of the earliest descriptions of Christians gathering on Sunday to break bread, the meal Catholics call the Eucharist, with a long sermon attached. Some things haven't changed in two thousand years.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` · `PAUL TALKS UNTIL MIDNIGHT.` · `ASLEEP, AND OUT THE WINDOW.` · `HIS LIFE IS IN HIM.` · then, large: `AND PAUL WENT ON UNTIL DAYBREAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive a long sermon. Settle, and breathe. Think of a speaker who tests your patience: a preacher, a teacher, a relative with long stories, a boss in meetings. Notice the impatience in your body. Now remember: the early Church sat through Paul until daybreak, and kept him. Picture that speaker as someone who has something they care about and maybe not the gift of brevity. Let a little of the irritation go. And if you're the long talker sometimes, smile at that too. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Eutychus. The young man whose name means fortunate, who fell asleep in a window during Paul's sermon, and was brought home alive. Today's word.

Your line: even paul went on. Today, give a long-winded person your patience. And that's week seventy-nine: sent, council, Lydia, midnight in the jail, the unknown god, tentmakers, and Eutychus. Day five hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics gather on Sunday, the first day of the week, for Mass, where the homily follows the Gospel and the Eucharist follows the homily; Sunday Mass is an obligation for Catholics.

original.note: Greek: Eutychus, a name meaning fortunate or lucky. a fitting name for a man who fell three stories.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funny story about a boring sermon.
what it means: the church gathers on Sunday to break bread, a young man falls and lives, and Paul goes right on until morning.
what a scholar hears: this is one of the earliest texts showing Christians meeting on the first day of the week to break bread. it sits in a 'we' passage, where the narrator says we were there.
